newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade car show glitter breaks economic gloom.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade car show glitter breaks economic gloom.

text.p: Thousands flocked to the Belgrade Fair on a warm and sunny Friday morning to see the latest car industry designs, while rare wealthy car-lovers queued up for luxury models making their debut in Belgrade.
The 36th International Motor Show failed to attract the hoped-for presence of foreign producers, whose new designs have been exhibited mainly by their local dealers.
Yugoslavia plans to further liberalise its trade regime to attract foreign businesses, a senior government official said opening the show.

"The government is ready to offer the best conditions to attract foreign companies and provide necessary legal guarantees. But any arrangement must be mutually beneficial and acceptable," said Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic.
Political and economic instability kept foreigners away from a market of 10 million consumers with declining purchasing power.
"A dying middle-class, reliant on its scarce and irregular monthly income, can hardly afford to change their old cars for new ones," head of the Belgrade Fair Sinisa Zaric told Reuters.
The average age of Yugoslav cars was 17 years and any fresh sales largely depended on consumer credit support from domestic banks, he said.
But the nouveaux riches, amassing wealth during years of U.N. sanctions, were ready to change their three or four year old cars for the latest designs.
A colourful display included Mercedes Benz with 16 models of its C, E and S class, commercial vehicles and buses.
Renault presents 11 models, with Megan Scenic and Renault Spider as the most attractive.
BMW exhibits BMW 5 Touring Estate and James Bond's BMW Z3 roadster. Volkswagen W came with new Passat 1.9 TDI and Audi with its latest A6 model, premiered at the Geneva Car Show.
The Belgrade show also attracted Mitsubishi, Suzuki, Subaru and Yamaha of Japan, Korea's Daewoo, India's Maruti and Tata, U.S. Chrysler, and Europe's Fiat, Opel, Ford, Skoda, Maserati, Volvo.
Taxes and customs duties on imported cars increase prices of foreign vehicles by as much as 84.4 percent.
Yugoslavia set a 1997 import quota at around 12,000 new vehicles, sharply up on 3,500 cars last year.
"Some 5,000-7,000 cars are destined for taxi associations and rent-a-car agencies, while the remainder is available for individual imports," Zaric said.
But freshly waxed and shiny exhibits remained beyond reach for most visitors, who live on an average $100 monthly income.
"Demand for imported cars is great. Only last year, up to 70,000 second-hand passenger cars entered the country," said Ljubivoje Todorovic of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce.
Cheaper second-hand cars, despite age and mileage offer more safety, comfort and efficiency than the new ones produced by the only local producer Zastava, traders said.
Zastava's most popular Yugo model cost around 7,000 German marks, but lacks quality to match the price, a car dealer said.
